extracted.intended_audience: chemical manufacturers, importers, distributors, label and SDS preparers, safety/compliance officers
extracted.subtask_description: Rules and guidance for preparing OSHA Hazard Communication Standard (HCS) labels and Safety Data Sheets (SDS), including selection, combination, and presentation of hazard and precautionary statements, PPE instructions, pictograms, and special-case labeling (e.g., combustible dust, corrosive to respiratory tract, aerosols, flammable gases).

rubrics_metrics.name: Combining and prioritizing repeated medical response statements
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘If the same medical response statement is triggered multiple times, the label need only include one precautionary statement reflecting the response at the highest level with the greatest urgency, which should always be combined with at least one route of exposure or symptom “IF” statement.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This revision (C.2.4.10(a)) is intended to simplify presentation while retaining the most important information for end users. It does not change C.2.2's requirement that all applicable hazard statements must appear on the label. Use combination/prioritization only when general principles are followed and the highest-urgency response is shown with at least one route/symptom 'IF' statement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mandatory separate listing of two specific medical response statements
rubrics_metrics.description: Where both the medical response precautionary statements 'Get medical advice/attention if you feel unwell' and 'Get immediate medical advice/attention' are applicable, they must both appear as separate statements on the label (C.2.4.10(c)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a limited exception to the combining/prioritizing allowance in (a) and (b). OSHA replaced 'should' with 'must' in C.2.4.10(c) to make clear that label preparers do not have discretion to combine these two statements into a single statement.

rubrics_metrics.name: SDS may mirror label medical statements (but may include more)
rubrics_metrics.description: The SDS is not required to include any more or different medical statements than are presented on the label; if the label is only required to have one medical response statement under C.2.4.10, then the SDS may also contain only that statement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: It is permissible, but not required, for SDS preparers to include additional medical response statements beyond those on the label.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alignment with GHS Rev. 7 for medical precautionary statements (Rev.8 optional)
rubrics_metrics.description: OSHA is finalizing C.2.4.10 in alignment with GHS Rev. 7, but label preparers may use the Rev. 8 precautionary statements in lieu of the Rev. 7 statements when the messaging directs users to similar actions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OSHA found Rev.7 and Rev.8 provide equivalent information to downstream users; adoption of Rev.7 was finalized because major trading partners align with Rev.7, but Rev.8 standardized statements are permissible where messaging is similar.

rubrics_metrics.name: Flammable gas category hazard statements
rubrics_metrics.description: Subdivide Category 1 flammable gases into categories 1A and 1B; require the hazard statement 'Extremely flammable gas' for Category 1A (including pyrophoric and chemically unstable gases) and 'Flammable gas' for Category 1B.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Additional hazard and precautionary statements are required to communicate hazards specific to pyrophoric and chemically unstable gases. OSHA adopts Rev.7 language (with minor editorial HCS terminology changes).

rubrics_metrics.name: Aerosols class and labeling elements
rubrics_metrics.description: Add non-flammable aerosols to the 'Aerosols' hazard class and adopt Rev.7 hazard/precautionary statements for non-flammable aerosols; where aerosols are labeled as gases under pressure, require the flame pictogram for Categories 1 and 2 (no pictogram for Category 3), signal word 'warning' (if 'danger' not required), and hazard statement 'pressurized container, may burst if heated.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These changes are intended to better differentiate hazards of non-flammable aerosols from gases under pressure and align HCS with GHS Rev.7; minor editorial term substitution (HCS terminology) applies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Desensitized explosives labeling
rubrics_metrics.description: Adopt pictogram, signal word, hazard statements, and precautionary statements for desensitized explosives from Rev.7 (added in Appendix C at C.4.30/C.4.31).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Label elements mirror Rev.7 to improve hazard communication for desensitized explosives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consolidation of acute toxicity—oral categories
rubrics_metrics.description: Consolidate hazard category information for C.4.1 (acute toxicity—oral) by deleting the table for Category 3 and combining Categories 1, 2, and 3 in one table because all three categories have the same precautionary statements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a formatting/conciseness change that does not affect substantive communication requirements for categories 1–3.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combustible dust hazard phrase options and bracketed text use
rubrics_metrics.description: Allow either 'May form combustible dust concentrations in air' or 'May form explosible dust-air mixture' as the hazard statement; bracketed text '[if small particles are generated during further processing, handling or by other means]' may be added when appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OSHA added explicit explanatory text: 'Text in square brackets may be used when the material can only create a combustible dust hazard due to the creation of small particles during the processing or handling of the chemical.' No new definitions for 'explosible' are provided; OSHA treats the terms as interchangeable for labeling purposes and refers to OSHA Publication 3644-04 for further discussion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pictogram single-instance rule
rubrics_metrics.description: Pictograms may only appear once on a label; if multiple hazards require the use of the same pictogram, it may not appear a second time on the label.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When multiple hazards call for the same pictogram, include that pictogram a single time and ensure associated hazard/precautionary statements communicate the multiple hazards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Labeling for 'corrosive to the respiratory tract'
rubrics_metrics.description: If a substance/mixture is determined to be corrosive to the respiratory tract, the corrosivity hazard must be communicated with the corrosion pictogram and the hazard statement 'corrosive to the respiratory tract.' For STOT SE Category 1, use 'corrosive to the respiratory tract, if inhaled' and the corrosion pictogram in lieu of the STOT hazard statement and health hazard pictogram.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OSHA added notes to Tables C.4.3, C.4.4, C.4.5 and C.4.11 to clarify required label elements when data (skin/eye/inhalation/STOT) indicate respiratory corrosivity. The STOT SE phrasing includes 'if inhaled' per A.8.2.1.2 route-identification requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: PPE instruction—specify type of equipment where appropriate
rubrics_metrics.description: Instruction accompanying 'Wear protective gloves/protective clothing' revised to read: 'Chemical manufacturer, importer, or distributor to specify type of equipment where appropriate.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Label preparers must specify the appropriate type of PPE when a specific type (e.g., 'PVC gloves', 'nitrile rubber gloves' with thickness/breakthrough time) is necessary to protect workers. A more general statement may be used only when a specific type is not needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inclusion (and exclusion) of hearing protection in PPE lists
rubrics_metrics.description: OSHA adopts expanded PPE phrasing in some prevention columns to include 'hearing protection' for hazards where hazardous noise is relevant (e.g., certain explosives, pyrophoric gases), but will not add 'hearing protection' for germ cell mutagenicity, carcinogenicity, and reproductive toxicity because it is not appropriate for those hazards.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The backslash '/' usage in C.2.4.2 allows label/SDS preparers to choose appropriate phrases. OSHA expects preparers not to include hearing protection for hazards where it is not protective; inclusion should match the hazard and avoid misuse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ellipses in PPE lists allow adding other PPE (e.g., respiratory protection)
rubrics_metrics.description: OSHA finalized ellipses at the end of PPE lists in prevention columns to allow addition of other types of PPE, including respiratory protection, where appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although the ellipses permit adding respiratory protection, OSHA did not propose or finalize making respiratory protection language mandatory in the cited hazard classes (these specific additions were out of scope for this rulemaking). Label preparers may add other PPE when warranted by the hazard.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement to include all applicable hazard statements (C.2.2)
rubrics_metrics.description: Nothing in paragraph C.2.4.10 changes the requirements of C.2.2 that all applicable hazard statements must appear on the label; producers are still required to include all hazards associated with their products under the HCS.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even when combining/prioritizing precautionary statements for clarity, ensure the label and SDS reflect all classifications and applicable hazard statements per C.2.2.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unknown acute toxicity percentage must specify route and appear on label and SDS (C.3.3)
rubrics_metrics.description: Where an ingredient with unknown acute toxicity is used in a mixture at a concentration >1 percent and the mixture is not classified based on testing of the mixture as a whole, a statement that 'X% of the mixture consists of ingredient(s) of unknown acute toxicity (oral/dermal/inhalation)' is required on the label and safety data sheet.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The percentage of unknown acute toxicity should be differentiated by route of exposure (oral/dermal/inhalation) because ingredients may have unknown toxicity for more than one route. OSHA will update guidance to clarify application.
